L0@P0: Near Optimal Bayesian Active Learning for Decision Making
L1@P0: Shervin Javdani Yuxin Chen Amin Karbasi
L2@P0: Carnegie Mellon University ETH Zürich ETH Zürich
L3@P0: Andreas Krause J. Andrew Bagnell Siddhartha Srinivasa
L4@P0: ETH Zürich Carnegie Mellon University Carnegie Mellon University
L5@P0: Abstract
L6@P0: How should we gather information to make effective decisions? We address Bayesian active
L7@P0: learning and experimental design problems,
L8@P0: where we sequentially select tests to reduce
L9@P0: uncertainty about a set of hypotheses. Instead
L10@P0: of minimizing uncertainty per se, we consider a
L11@P0: set of overlapping decision regions of these hypotheses. Our goal is to drive uncertainty into
L12@P0: a single decision region as quickly as possible.
L13@P0: We identify necessary and sufficient conditions for correctly identifying a decision region
L14@P0: that contains all hypotheses consistent with
L15@P0: observations. We develop a novel Hyperedge
L16@P0: Cutting (HEC) algorithm for this problem,
L17@P0: and prove that is competitive with the intractable optimal policy. Our efficient implementation of the algorithm relies on computing subsets of the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials. Finally, we demonstrate
L18@P0: its effectiveness on two practical applications:
L19@P0: approximate comparison-based learning and
L20@P0: active localization using a robot manipulator.
L21@P0: 1 Introduction
L22@P0: Bayesian active learning addresses the problem of
L23@P0: selecting a sequence of experiments, or tests, to
L24@P0: determine a hypothesis consistent with observations.
L25@P0: This fundamental problem arises in a wide range
L26@P0: of applications such as medical procedures, content
L27@P0: search, and robotics. It has been studied in several
L28@P0: domains, including machine learning (Dasgupta, 2004;
L29@P0: Balcan et al., 2006; Nowak, 2009), statistics (LindAppearing in Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS)
L30@P0: 2014, Reykjavik, Iceland. JMLR: W&CP volume 33.
L31@P0: Copyright 2014 by the authors.
L32@P0: ley, 1956; Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995), decision
L33@P0: theory (Howard, 1966), and others.
L34@P0: For instance, in automated medical diagnosis (Kononenko, 2001) we are presented with hypotheses about the state of a patient, and select
L35@P0: medical tests to infer their illness. In comparison-based
L36@P0: learning (Goyal et al., 2008; Karbasi et al., 2012), we
L37@P0: infer a target in a database by sequentially presenting
L38@P0: a user with pairs of candidates, and having the user
L39@P0: select which is closer. In robotic active localization,
L40@P0: the robot attempts to identify its own or an object’s
L41@P0: location by probing, e.g., with touch or vision (Fox
L42@P0: et al., 1998; Kollar and Roy, 2008; Hsiao et al., 2008;
L43@P0: Javdani et al., 2013). In general, the goal is to gather
L44@P0: the necessary information while minimizing test cost.
L45@P0: In this paper, we develop a general framework for
L46@P0: addressing these problems. Instead of indiscriminately
L47@P0: minimizing uncertainty about hypotheses directly, we
L48@P0: aim to reduce uncertainty in a structured way to facilitate decision making. We suppose the hypothesis space
L49@P0: is covered by a set of decision regions: Each region identifies the set of hypotheses for which it would succeed.
L50@P0: Our goal is to select tests that quickly concentrate all
L51@P0: consistent hypotheses in a single decision region.
L52@P0: Special cases of this general problem have been studied.
L53@P0: In the so called Optimal Decision Tree (ODT) problem,
L54@P0: each decision region corresponds to a single hypothesis.
L55@P0: In this case, a greedy algorithm called Generalized
L56@P0: Binary Search (GBS) is known to perform near
L57@P0: optimally, i.e., the expected number of observations
L58@P0: is O(log n) more than the optimum policy where n
L59@P0: indicates the number of hypotheses (Dasgupta, 2004;
L60@P0: Guillory and Bilmes, 2009; Kosaraju and Borgstrom,
L61@P0: 1999). GBS greedily selects tests in expectation over
L62@P0: the test outcomes to maximize the probability mass
L63@P0: of eliminated hypotheses. Another special instance

L29@P1: Abstract. Account access graphs have been proposed as a way to model
L30@P1: relationships between user credentials, accounts, and methods of access;
L31@P1: they capture both multiple simultaneous access routes (e.g., for multifactor authentication) as well as multiple alternative access routes (e.g.,
L32@P1: for account recovery). In this paper we extend the formalism with state
L33@P1: transitions and tactics. State transitions capture how access may change
L34@P1: over time as users or adversaries use access routes and add or remove
L35@P1: credentials and accounts. Tactics allow us to model and document attacker techniques or resilience strategies, by writing small programs. We
L36@P1: illustrate these ideas using some attacks against mobile authentication
L37@P1: and banking applications which have been publicised in 2023.
L38@P1: Keywords: account access graphs, tactics, security, Android, iOS
L39@P1: 1 Introduction
L40@P1: As the connections between online services we use in our daily lives increase, so
L41@P1: do the possibilities for an attacker to exploit them. By chaining a series of access
L42@P1: escalations, often using recovery or fallback methods, an attacker can take over
L43@P1: more and more of a user’s accounts. A prominent example of such an account
L44@P1: takeover attack was in 2012 when the Wired journalist Mat Honan’s Twitter account was compromised in a sequence of steps in which an attacker took control
L45@P1: of his Amazon account, Apple account, Google account and eventually the coveted Twitter account [10]. Several analogous attacks have arisen over the years
L46@P1: following similar procedural steps [6,13,15]. Attacks that abuse a particular constellation of user accounts are difficult to eliminate because different users have
L47@P1: different and continuously changing account ecosystems.
L48@P1: Attackers use multiple strategies and build complex attacks by combining
L49@P1: smaller steps. To understand and prevent attacks it helps to catalogue vulnerabilities and reduce complex attacks to their constituent building blocks. This
L50@P1: approach is seen elsewhere. For software vulnerabilities, for example, the Metasploit Framework [11] provides a scripting language so penetration testers can
L51@P1: combine known exploits with scanning tools.
L52@P1: In this paper we provide ways to model and catalogue account takeover attacks and their defences. To do this we propose a generic language of attack

L8@P0: Abstract. This paper introduces arithmetic sketching, an abstraction
L9@P0: of a primitive that several previous works use to achieve lightweight,
L10@P0: low-communication zero-knowledge verification of secret-shared vectors.
L11@P0: An arithmetic sketching scheme for a language L ⊆ F
L12@P0: n
L13@P0: consists of (1)
L14@P0: a randomized linear function compressing a long input x to a short
L15@P0: “sketch,” and (2) a small arithmetic circuit that accepts the sketch if
L16@P0: and only if x ∈ L, up to some small error. If the language L has an
L17@P0: arithmetic sketching scheme with short sketches, then it is possible to test
L18@P0: membership in L using an arithmetic circuit with few multiplication gates.
L19@P0: Since multiplications are the dominant cost in protocols for computation
L20@P0: on secret-shared, encrypted, and committed data, arithmetic sketching
L21@P0: schemes give rise to lightweight protocols in each of these settings.
L22@P0: Beyond the formalization of arithmetic sketching, our contributions are:
L23@P0: – A general framework for constructing arithmetic sketching schemes
L24@P0: from algebraic varieties. This framework unifies schemes from prior
L25@P0: work and gives rise to schemes for useful new languages and with
L26@P0: improved soundness error.
L27@P0: – The first arithmetic sketching schemes for languages of sparse vectors:
L28@P0: vectors with bounded Hamming weight, bounded L1 norm, and
L29@P0: vectors whose few non-zero values satisfy a given predicate.
L30@P0: – A method for “compiling” any arithmetic sketching scheme for a
L31@P0: language L into a low-communication malicious-secure multi-server
L32@P0: protocol for securely testing that a client-provided secret-shared
L33@P0: vector is in L.
L34@P0: We also prove the first nontrivial lower bounds showing limits on the
L35@P0: sketch size for certain languages (e.g., vectors of Hamming-weight one)
L36@P0: and proving the non-existence of arithmetic sketching schemes for others
L37@P0: (e.g., the language of all vectors that contain a specific value).
L38@P0: 1 Introduction
L39@P0: In many cryptographic protocols, a server holds an encoding of a large clientprovided vector. To protect against client misbehavior, the server must test
L40@P0-1: whether the vector satisfies a simple predicate. For example:– In private ad measurement [29, 48], an aggregation server holds a linearly
L41@P1: homomorphic encryption of a client-provided vector; the server must test
L42@P1: that the encrypted vector is zero everywhere except with a “1” at a single
L43@P1: location.
L44@P1: – In PIR writing [42] and private messaging [1, 17, 24], a set of servers holds
L45@P1: additive secret shares of a client-provided vector; the servers must test that
L46@P1: the secret-shared vector is zero everywhere except that it contains an arbitrary
L47@P1: value at a single location.
L48@P1: – In private-aggregation [10,16,20,36,45], a set of servers holds a secret-sharing
L49@P1: of a large client-provided vector; the server must test whether the vector has
L50@P1: bounded Hamming weight.
L51@P1: – In e-voting schemes [31], a tally server holds a linearly homomorphic encryption of a vector representing a ballot; the server must test that the vector
L52@P1: has non-negative entries and bounded L1 norm.
L53@P1: – In verifiable distributed multi-point functions [21], a set of servers holds
L54@P1: (compressed) additive secret shares of a client-provided vector; the servers
L55@P1: must test whether the vector has Hamming weight exactly w.
L56@P1: – In protocols for malicious-secure OT and MPC [19], a verifier holds a linearly
L57@P1: homomorphic commitment to a prover-provided vector; the verifier must test
L58@P1: whether the vector has bounded Hamming weight.
